beats.beat: Mrs Pike arranges for Louisa to ride with Rowe to Bramdean to fetch the mason's estimate, meaning further matchmaking, but Louisa is occupied writing to her uncle and sends word she cannot go.
Judith, already walking to the draper's for thread, is asked to carry the errand instead, and Mrs Pike, absorbed in Louisa's letter, waves her off without thinking of a chaperone.
A mile past the mill the donkey cart's wheel splits, and Rowe and Judith are left stranded on the verge waiting for someone to pass.
Sitting together the better part of an hour, they finally say aloud what each believed of the other, the sermon and the novels, and find both accounts had grown larger with telling.
A farmer's cart takes them up at last, but by the time they reach Amberlight the light is failing, and the green is not empty.

turn.note: Ends on the green not empty, coach in, Mrs Hale watching from the library window, priming chapter 5's gossip.

continuity: Chapter 2 states of Rowe and the novel list: 'He had not, and said so, and thought no more about it.' Chapter 4 has him say 'I was ashamed of the word I used before I reached the lych gate, and I have never said so aloud until this minute' — a persistent private shame the earlier chapter explicitly denied he carried. Keep the chapter 2 account (indifference at the time) and revise chapter 4's line to something like 'I told myself I had thought no more of it' so the admission is a correction of self-deception rather than a contradicted fact.

generic_prose.quote: There was nothing to do but wait.
generic_prose.replace_with: fine as a short beat but pair with a concrete detail of the wait, e.g. what the donkey was doing, to avoid it reading as filler

trope_note: Serves all three declared tropes directly: the enmity is dismantled through the confessions on the verge, Mrs Pike's meddling is shown misfiring exactly as the outline promises, and the chaperone's absence is stated in free indirect discourse rather than narrated as incident.
fixes: Resolve the motive contradiction: change Rowe's line about carrying shame since January to acknowledge he had told himself otherwise at the time, matching chapter 2's 'thought no more about it.'

Trim the recap of Fenner/Bramdean/donkey-cart logistics in the Mrs Pike paragraph — these facts were established in chapter 1 and can be compressed to one sentence to bring the chapter closer to its 570-word target.
Consider giving 'There was nothing to do but wait' one concrete anchor (the donkey, the split spoke) rather than leaving it as a flat generic beat.

writer_note:
This story is now read by a single narrator rather than a
cast with a voice each, so the prose has to carry who is speaking. It was
written under the old rule, which forbade attribution because the voices made it
redundant.

Go through the chapter and add attribution wherever a listener — who cannot see
the page, and cannot look back — would lose track of who is speaking. A tag
belongs in its own narrator segment: `said Mrs Pike`, `Rowe said`, or an action
that does the same work: *Rowe turned the note over.* Two people alternating in
a plain exchange do not need one every line; the third turn usually does, and so
does every return to dialogue after narration, and every line in a scene of
three or more.

Do not attribute every line. An unbroken column of `said X` is padding, and it
is the opposite failure.

Where a line would be misread without it, you may add a `tag` to that segment —
`"[quietly]"`, `"[a beat]"`, `"[warmly]"` — as performance direction for the
voice. It is never printed and never spoken. A few a chapter at most, and never
to imitate a different person: one voice reads everyone.

Come back no longer than you started. These chapters are already at or over
their word ceiling, and attribution adds words — so take them back out of
restatement: a line of dialogue that lands followed by narration explaining that
it landed, a room established twice. If you come back long the check sends the
chapter straight back to be cut, which spends a revision on arithmetic instead
of on the prose.

Change nothing else. Same events, same beats, same jokes, same last line.
